bib.title: Instance-Dependent Lower Bounds (Chapter 16, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Book chapter, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press)

question: What is the best regret a consistent policy can achieve on a specific bandit instance, asymptotically and in finite time?
contributions: Definition of consistency and a generic asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound (Thm 16.2) for unstructured classes
Table of d_inf for Gaussian, Bernoulli, uniform families
A finite-time instance-dependent lower bound for Gaussian bandits (Lemma 16.3, Thm 16.4)

results.claim: Thm 16.2: for any consistent policy over an unstructured class E = M1 x ... x Mk, liminf R_n/log n is at least c*(nu,E) = sum over suboptimal arms of Delta_i / d_inf(P_i, mu*, M_i).
results.setup: Unstructured class of stochastic bandits, consistent policy, every nu in E; d_inf(P,mu*,M)=inf over P' in M of D(P,P') s.t. mu(P')>mu*
results.note: Stated in general form (Eq. 16.2); the chapter does not print the 2/Delta_i specialisation. Table 16.1 gives d_inf=(mu-mu*)^2/(2 sigma^2) for Gaussian with known variance, so for unit variance Delta_i/d_inf = 2/Delta_i (derived by the reader, not printed).

results.claim: Proof step: for each suboptimal arm i, liminf E[T_i(n)]/log n >= 1/d_i, via Bretagnolle-Huber (Thm 14.2) and divergence decomposition (Lemma 15.1), then regret decomposition Lemma 4.5.
results.setup: As Thm 16.2; alternative bandit nu' with P'_i having D(P_i,P'_i)<=d_i+eps and mean above mu*; event A={T_i(n)>n/2}

results.claim: Asymptotic optimality is defined as lim R_n/log n = c*(nu,E) for all nu in E (Eq. 16.3); UCB (Ch. 8) is asymptotically optimal for Gaussian unit-variance E_N^k(1) and KL-UCB (Ch. 10) for Bernoulli E_B^k.
results.setup: Classes E_N^k(1) (Gaussian, unit variance) and E_B^k (Bernoulli)
results.note: The text says 'UCB from Chapter 8' without naming a variant; the asymptotically optimal UCB is the one analysed in Ch. 8 (not checked here).

results.claim: Thm 16.4 finite-time bound for Gaussian bandits: if R_n(pi,nu')<=C n^p for all n in N and all nu' in E(nu), then for any eps in (0,1], R_n(pi,nu) >= 2/(1+eps)^2 * sum_{i:Delta_i>0} ((1-p)log n + log(eps Delta_i/(8C)))^+ / Delta_i.
results.setup: nu in E_N^k Gaussian bandit; E(nu)={nu' in E_N^k : mu_i(nu') in [mu_i, mu_i+2 Delta_i]}; constants C>0, p in (0,1); N nonempty subset of naturals
results.note: The text prints 'Delta_i' dividing the bracket; the (.)^+ extraction is garbled, so read the typeset form in the book for placement of the positive part.

results.claim: For p = 1/2 the leading term of the Thm 16.4 bound is about half the asymptotic bound; the authors say this effect may be real since the policy class is larger.
results.quote: When p = 1/2, the leading term in this lower bound is approximately half that

results.claim: ETC and elimination-based algorithms cannot be asymptotically optimal; however tuned they pay an extra factor of two on standard Gaussian bandits (Garivier et al. 2016b).
results.setup: Standard Gaussian bandit problems, versus optimal asymptotic regret
results.quote: must incur an additional multiplicative penalty of a factor of two

results.claim: Consistency alone allows playing A_t=1 for the first 10^100 rounds, so it cannot give non-asymptotic bounds.
results.note: Printed '10100' by extraction; it is 10^100 as typeset.

limits: Asymptotic and unstructured-class only: with structure, a policy can learn about one arm from others and regret falls (Note 2); structured lower bounds are left to later chapters.
Consistency is asymptotic, so Thm 16.2 says nothing about finite n; Thm 16.4 needs a polynomial minimax-style regret bound over a neighbourhood E(nu).
Table 16.1 covers parametric families only; non-parametric classes are largely open, with exceptions in Honda & Takemura (2010, 2015) and Lattimore (2017).
For unknown subgaussian constant, d_inf=0 and consistent policies have infinite lower bound (Ex 16.4).
Chapter has no experiments; no figure beyond conceptual Fig 16.1.

terms.definition: A policy pi is consistent over a class E if for all nu in E and p>0, lim R_n(pi,nu)/n^p = 0; the class is denoted Pi_cons(E).
A class E = M1 x ... x Mk with M1..Mk sets of distributions.
d_inf(P,mu*,M) = inf over P' in M of {D(P,P') : mu(P')>mu*}, for P in M with mu(P)<mu*.
A policy with lim R_n(pi,nu)/log n = c*(nu,E) for all nu in E (Eq. 16.3).

lineage.note: ETC and elimination cannot reach asymptotic optimality (factor 2)

figures.caption: On the x-axis, the instances are ordered according to the measure of difficulty, and the y-axis shows the regret (on some scale). In the previous chapter, we proved that no policy can be entirely below the horizontal 'minimax optimal' line. Theorem 16.4 in this chapter show that if the regret of a policy is below the 'instance optimal' line at any point, then it must have regret above the shaded region for other instances. For example, the 'over-specialized' policy.
figures.why: Shows the trade-off: beating the instance-optimal line on one instance costs regret on others.

figures.caption: Expressions for dinf for different parametric families when the mean of P is less than mu*.
figures.why: Gives d_inf for Gaussian known variance ((mu-mu*)^2/(2 sigma^2)), Gaussian unknown variance, Bernoulli, uniform.
